doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Hazel Scott, Adelaide Hall, Reginald Foresythe and Leslie Hutchinson
summary: She remembers jazzing-the-classics pianist Hazel Scott, singers Adelaide Hall and Elisabeth Welch, mentor Reginald Foresythe, and her crush on the singer Leslie Hutchinson, whose repertoire she learned backstage.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Well, Hazel. Hazel Scott. I used to listen to her when she was in her bag of doing . . . jazzing the classics. At the time that I listened to that, I thought that was very hip. I was still in England, hearing those things.
Did you know her husband, Adam Clayton Powell.
I met him. Yeah, and I met his son too.
Who’s still very prominent in the New York . . .

I’m trying to think. There were a couple of English pianists, and there were a couple of American people that I met when I was in vaudeville, who had originally come from here, like Adelaide Hall. I became very friendly with her. Years ago, Elizabeth Welsh. I don’t know if that name would mean anything to you. Elizabeth Welsh had a piano player who wrote . . . Reginald Foresythe. How about that name!
Wow. Tell the listeners who Elizabeth Welsh was. Was she a vocalist or . . .

Elizabeth Welsh was a very . . . I guess she had gone to England from America. She was a very fine singer. A pop singer, like probably the Diana Ross of her day. And of course Adelaide Hall I think is well known to all jazz people.
Didn’t Art Tatum accompany her at one . . .

He might have. Yeah. But Reginald Foresythe was a . . . I guess you’d call him a pianist who wrote these very sophisticated novelty piano pieces. He did one called “Dodging A Divorcee.” It was the name of one of them. I used to play these things, and I thought he was fabulous. He was the accompanist for Elizabeth Welsh. I used to hang about back stage so I could hear him play, and he’d talk to me. He was a mentor, come to think of it. I hadn’t thought about him for years.

Maybe Hazel and Cleo Brown and of course James P. Johnson and Fats . . . Duke was over there in England, but I was too inhibited among . . . they were . . . they would never let me go anywhere to hear anybody. It didn’t even occur to me to go, like kids do nowadays and then show up back stage. There was a singer that that you may have heard of. Leslie Hutchinson. Hutch, they called him. Very popular singer. I had a big crush on him. Bobby Short always laughs when he hears that.
Well, he probably knows that Hutch was not really one for girls.
But he was terribly attractive, and sang all these love songs. Women swooned.
What was his name again, so the listeners with their . . .
I learned a lot that I can play from his repertoire, hanging back stage and hearing him perform.
